newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish inflation highlights need for stability.
newsitem.headline: Turkish inflation highlights need for stability.

text.p: Turkey's need for a medium-term economic plan was underscored on Tuesday by higher-than-expected inflation figures for January, analysts said.

Financial markets are looking for signs of easing inflation in coming months if they are to retain confidence in the government's ability to deliver on its bold promises to restore stability to public finances.

Turkish shares fell 3.62 percent in the morning after news of a 5.6 percent month-on-month rise in wholesale prices and a 5.9 percent leap in consumer prices during January after forecasts of a 4.0 to 5.3 percent rise.

Shares extended their losses in the afternoon to close 6.98 percent down. But later selling was mainly due to political worries, with tensions between the Islamist-led government and the secularist army, and a leftist bid to topple the government with a censure motion.

Against a background of just under 80 percent year-on-year inflation, analysts say pushing through a stability programme requires the stimulus of an accord with International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials, who are expected to visit Turkey in March.
"In terms of credibility in the international markets reaching an accord with the IMF is important," said Atilla Yesilada, director of research at Global Securities.
There is speculation that Ankara will implement a new IMF-sponsored economic programme.
A previous plan, put in place following a financial crisis in 1994, was abandoned after about 17 months.
Turkish central bank governor Gazi Ercel this week stressed the importance of a medium-term economic programme to combat inflation and other economic ills.
"With the IMF or without the IMF, the Turkish authorities should at least address...inflation," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

He said the government should also deal with structural issues such as broadening the tax base and the problems of the social security system to build on signs of progress since the Islamist-led coalition came to power last June.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has raised expectations on the economy with a balanced budget plan for 1997 and forecasts of multi-billion dollar privatisation revenues and sharply lower inflation in the medium-term.

Adding to the positive scenario, bond yields have plunged by some 30 percentage points since late 1996 to 80-81 percent amid increased liquidity and a rise in witholding tax on interest income from state securities.
Shares have surged 50.1 percent since the start of the year, boosted by a court ruling facilitating the sale of Turk Telekom and by a lower-than-expected 1996 budget deficit.

However, the budget deficit, amounting to 1,215 trillion lira ($10.4 billion), remains a heavy burden on the economy. Adding to the burden is a current account deficit which rose sharply to $2.31 billion in the first half of 1996.

The pressure on public finances is reflected in foreign debt repayments, with the Treasury and public institutions expected to service around $8 billion this year, compared with fresh borrowing on international markets of at least $2 billion.
"This situation cannot be sustained for ever where money is being sucked out of the country," Yesilada said.

Privatisation remains a key source of badly-needed revenues for Erbakan's government, but despite the positive court ruling on Turk Telekom doubts have arisen about the level of buying interest in many Turkish state enterprises.
A tender for the sale of a 30-40 percent stake in leading flat steel producer Erdemir attracted only two bids.

As the IMF visit looms, the other major concern is whether the government can focus on its economic priorities in the face apparent tensions between Erbakan's party and its conservative alliance partners over recent Islamist proposals on building mosques and the wearing of headscarves by public employees.
Analysts say there is a risk that such populist moves could distract government attention away from the discipline needed to deal with an overhaul of the economy.
